You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 5 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 5 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

structured_output.failure_statement: Agent declares a migration or fix complete and stops before running (or without waiting for the result of) the verification step the task itself requires — a check command, a test suite, or a required changelog — so the user discovers the unmet requirement only after being told it was done.

remedy_content.new_body: Before reporting any task, fix, or migration as complete, run its declared verification step — test suite, check command, required changelog, or other stated acceptance criterion — and report the actual result plainly. Never claim a task is done ahead of that check, and never soften a failing or unrun check into a completion claim.

structured_output.routing_rationale: All three promoted incidents (11, 12, 31) are the same failure mode already targeted by the existing global rule R2 ("Fake Release Discipline"): the agent reports a migration/fix as complete without first running the declared verification step (a check command in 11/12, a required changelog in 31), and the user has to point out the check never ran or never passed. R2 already encodes the exact right behavior ("run its declared verification command and report the result plainly") but is scoped narrowly to "release," so it doesn't literally cover a migration or a generic fix. Rather than add a sibling skill or claude-md block duplicating R1's or R2's purpose, the cheapest fix is to broaden R2's wording from "release" to "any task/fix/migration," and explicitly include non-command verification artifacts like a required changelog so incident 31 is covered too. R1 (skill fake-verify-before-claim) addresses the same theme but at higher cost (a skill vs. a two-line standing rule); since the required fix here is just widening scope, not adding new procedural steps, the one-line claude-md revision is preferred over touching or duplicating the skill. R3-R5 are pending proposals about unrelated failure modes (destructive-deletion confirmation, wrong branch/environment, output scope mismatch) and don't overlap.
